name: Act of July 1, 1892 restoring the north half of the Colville Reservation to the public domain
nations: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation
promises: Not a treaty. Under the May 9, 1891 agreement the tribes were to cede the north half of the reservation in return for $1,500,000 in five instalments and the promise in Article 6 that their right to hunt and fish on unallotted ceded land would not be taken away; the agreement was to take effect only on congressional approval (Antoine v. Washington).

breaches.what: Congress declared the north half vacated and restored to the public domain 'notwithstanding any executive order' and opened it to settlement. It did not provide the $1,500,000 the 1891 agreement promised: sale proceeds were held subject to future appropriation and spent at the Secretary's discretion, and section 8 said nothing in the Act recognized the Indians' title. The payment was authorized only in 1906. The Indian Claims Commission concluded in 1975 that the tribes' title to the north half was extinguished by this Act.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Act of July 1, 1892, ch. 140, 27 Stat. 62, secs. 1, 2 and 8; Indian Claims Commission, Docket 181-C, conclusions of law of June 13, 1975 (36 Ind. Cl. Comm. 183); payment history as set out in Antoine v. Washington, 420 U.S. 194 (1975)

source.title: Act of July 1, 1892, ch. 140, 27 Stat. 62 (opening of part of the Colville Reservation)

landTaken: The north half of the reservation, Royce area 717; the Act described it as about 1,500,000 acres (see cession-1872-07-02-methow-okanagan).
compensation: The Act of June 21, 1906 authorized $1,500,000, paid in five appropriations of $300,000 from 1907 to 1911 (Antoine v. Washington). Reservation claims, including the north half, were settled in Indian Claims Commission Dockets 181-A and 181-B for $3,500,000 in 1967 (see the primary record).
today: In Antoine v. Washington (1975) the Supreme Court held that Congress, by ratifying the 1891 agreement, preserved the tribes' Article 6 hunting and fishing rights on the ceded north half against state regulation.

treaties.json lists no present-day tribe for this row; the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation are the successors. Royce lists two areas: 717 (the ceded north half) and 718 (the diminished reservation). Not edited.

Antoine v. Washington (1975) counts the 1892 Act as the first of the statutes by which Congress approved the 1891 agreement; the primary record relies on the Indian Claims Commission's summary of the petitioners' claim that it was not ratified. The breach stands on the opening without the promised payment.
The Colville Tribes' own account of the north half was not located.

Audit 2026-11-08 (round 14): breach reworded against the Act and Antoine. The Antoine majority treats the 1892 Act as the first of the statutes by which Congress approved the 1891 agreement (the dissent stresses section 8), so the breach no longer reads as a refusal to ratify; it rests on the Act's own text (vacated notwithstanding the executive order, proceeds held at Congress's disposal, title not recognized, no $1,500,000) and the Commission's 1975 conclusion that the Act extinguished the north-half title. The breach source is now the Act; Antoine stays in sources. The Commission's order gives the Act's date as June 20, 1892, the day the President received it; it became law without signature and Royce and Antoine date it July 1, 1892.

Audit 2026-11-08 (round 14): lead: Docket 181-C ended in a Court of Claims judgment of $3,397,874 on January 23, 1981 (226 Ct. Cl. 725, a one-line entry); the 1975 order made the United States liable for resources removed from the north half before 1892 with its aid. Whether any of that judgment concerns the north half was not traced.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. In 1891 the Colville tribes agreed to give up the north half of their reservation for $1,500,000, keeping hunting and fishing rights there.
plain.happened: In 1892 Congress opened the north half to settlers without providing the promised payment, and said it did not recognize the tribes' title. Congress authorized the money only in 1906, fourteen years later.
plain.today: The $1,500,000 was paid from 1907 to 1911. In 1975 the Supreme Court upheld the tribes' hunting and fishing rights on the north half.
